1:
The trumpet is a priestly duty with two possible objects. Gill addresses it to the priests, whose business it was to blow for solemn assemblies at the temple mount, and describes the manner: a broken quivering note giving notice of danger from the locusts or the enemies they signify, that the people might return by repentance. Wesley agrees, the exhortation continuing to the priests. Henry allows both directions the summons might take: to call the invading army together, the trumpet sounding a charge, or rather to give Judah notice so they might prepare to meet their God and endeavour by prayers and tears, the church's best artillery, to put the stroke by. He fixes the judgment in the law, among the plagues of Egypt.

Ellicott reads the summons as an intensification. Behind the locusts, exemplified by them, is a more terrible visitation: the prophet sees a mustering of nations bent on destroying his people, so the priests are to stir them up for a fast and for the defence of the land. The locusts have done their symbolic work; the day of the Lord is not merely approaching but imminent. Keil and Delitzsch place the passage structurally, denying this is a fresh address: it forms the second part of one sermon of repentance, repeating a command already hinted at in the previous chapter, giving the reason in a picture of the approaching judgment-day, and adding the assurance that the Lord will still take compassion if they return with the whole heart. Clarke gives the plan of the chapter and marks the transition at the end to the outpouring of the Spirit, so explained by one of the apostles. Calvin explains why he treats eleven verses together: their design is to stir the people by fear and make them sensible it was no time for rest, the Lord having long tolerated their wickedness and being now resolved to pour out his fury in full torrent.

The darkness of the day is glossed from natural history by two and from usage by two others. Gill takes it as alluding to the gloom the locusts cause, coming in such numbers as to darken the air; he cites travellers for their flying like a cloud and hiding the sun at noonday, and adds that the phrases may equally express great calamities, which scripture often signifies by darkness as prosperity by light. Clarke brings a traveller's report of locusts in Barbary, much bigger than the common grasshopper, with brown spotted wings and bodies of a bright yellow, appearing at the end of March after a long south wind. Calvin takes the darkness as extinguishing hope: light in scripture designates a cheerful state or the hope of deliverance, so calling the day dark declares there is no hope of restoration. Wesley reads it as a time of great troubles alluding to the last day.

The morning spread on the mountains divides them, and the division is lexical. Calvin takes the figure for speed, the dawn spreading in a moment over the mountains where darkness had been. Wesley reads it the same way and extends it: as the morning spreads over the whole hemisphere and first on the high mountains, so shall the calamities overspread this people; he identifies the great people as more directly the Babylonians. Ellicott argues the opposite from the root. The Hebrew for morning comes from a verb meaning both to become black and to break forth as light; from the second comes the word for dawn, from the first the word for blackness which gives the Nile its name. He thinks it more in harmony with the context to take the sense of blackness and understand a thick dark cloud settled on the mountain top; the description following, he holds, comprehends equally the natural and the political locust. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering, morning dawn spread over the mountains.
3:
The fire before and behind is read literally by most. Gill denies it means the sun's heat or the drought, and makes the creatures themselves the consuming fire: they devoured grass and herbs and leaves as fire devours stubble, sucking out the moisture so that what they left shrivelled as though scorched. Clarke supplies three travellers' testimonies: that they consume like a conflagration and burn trees for two years after, that their leavings seem parched with fire, and that after the herbage they attack even the buds. Ellicott makes the application in a line: as with the locusts so with the invading hosts, the country found a paradise and left a desert. Wesley identifies the fire with the Chaldeans. Calvin takes the verse as announcing finality: God had chastised in various ways without advantage, so the last stroke remained, and he would wholly destroy men whom moderate punishments had not restored to a sound mind.

The likeness to horses is the best-attested observation. Gill reports two Jewish commentators referring it to their running, with the swiftness of horses rushing into battle, and adds from a scholar he names that the head of a locust is shaped like a horse's, a father of the church confirming it on examination. Clarke gives the same from a naturalist, quoting the Latin that they have an oblong head like a horse's bending downward, and notes that the Italians therefore call them cavalry; he adds a list from an Arabic writer in which the locust resembles ten animals. Ellicott finds the same comparison in the apocalypse, the shapes of the locusts like horses prepared for battle and the sound of their wings like chariots. Calvin declines the natural history and takes the verse for the suddenness of the vengeance: distance would be no obstacle, and the Jews were deceived by it into expecting a long respite.

The noise of chariots produces a lexical dispute. Calvin reports that some expound the word as chariots while the Hebrews take it for harness, and prefers chariots, since a comparison to horse-trappings would not suit a sound; the mountain tops are named because noise is great there. Gill explains the leaping from the anatomy, the hindmost legs being longest, citing a naturalist for the rule that insects with long hind legs leap.

The blackness of faces is where the philology thickens. Ellicott sets out three renderings: that they withdraw their ruddiness and grow pale, that they draw their colour into themselves, or that they contract a livid character; and he records the marginal alternative, adopted by the Greek and Latin versions and by a reformer, which reads pot instead, on the similarity of the two Hebrew words. Wesley describes the colour directly: that of dead men, or the dark paleness of those frightened into swoons. Gill compares the pain to a woman in travail: they might justly fear that all the fruits of the earth would be devoured and nothing left to live on, and the invading army filled them with the same consternation. Calvin draws the political inference: the invaders would by their fame alone lay all people prostrate, so the Jews could not resist.

On the discipline of the ranks they agree. Gill has them run like men of war, and cites a scholar quoting a Greek writer for their manner of fighting, that they strike not standing but running. Clarke enters a caution worth noting: the prophet does not say they are men of war but that they resemble them, for they are locusts and only in their operations like the rest. Wesley reads the skill in ordering and steadiness in rank, exactly like trained soldiers, as foretelling the terror and strength both of the armies signified and of the locusts. Keil and Delitzsch mark the comparison as running through these verses, the locust army likened throughout to a well-ordered host.
8:
The unbroken order of the march is glossed by all and given a soldier's reason by one. Gill takes the clause to mean that none presses on another or in the least hinders his progress. Calvin makes the point concrete: they would come in perfect order so the multitude created no confusion, which is rare, since an army can hardly march without tumult as two or three men walk together, and when a hundred horsemen move together some commonly hinder others.

That they are not wounded when they fall upon the sword divides the literal from the figurative. Clarke gives both: they have hard scales like a coat of mail, but the expression refers to the uselessness of all means to prevent their depredations. Wesley reads it verified twice over, literally in the locusts and again in the strange preservations of the invaders in their desperate adventures.

The running through the city is applied to the siege by three. Gill has them leap from place to place as locusts do, and as the Chaldeans did when they became masters of the city, running to seize their spoil. Wesley, who elsewhere calls the shaking a divine hyperbole, makes the distinction sharply: running to and fro suits not insects but soldiers who conquer a city and search everywhere for plunder, running on the wall to clear it, entering houses forsaken or defended, and coming in at the windows like a thief. Calvin draws the moral against false confidence: the Jews trusted in vain in their fortified cities, since the enemy would penetrate them as though there were no gates, though Judea abounded in cities that seemed impregnable and had often forced great armies to desist.

The shaking of earth and heaven is where the tile finds its one methodological dispute. Ellicott reports that some call the description a specimen of the highly wrought hyperbolical features of Hebrew poetry, and rejects the label: it is the presence and judgment of God, his voice in the thunder, that causes the trepidation. Calvin grants the hyperbole and defends it. The prophet speaks more hyperbolically, but he addressed men extremely stupid, so it behoved him to speak unusually to touch their feelings; it avails nothing to speak ordinarily to perverse men, especially those who have divested themselves of all shame and whom Satan has fascinated so that they fear nothing. Clarke calls the expressions poetical and turns them prettily: the earth quaked to see itself deprived of its verdure, the heavens trembled to lose their light; he adds from a scholar he names that their multitude is sometimes so immense as to obscure the heavens for twelve miles.

Whose army is uttered before is answered variously. Gill allows the locusts themselves, noting that a Roman naturalist called them the plague of the gods and the Arabians style them the army of God, and reports a tradition of theirs about an inscription on their backs and wings. Wesley takes it of both, the locusts and the Chaldeans signified by them, God summoning and encouraging them as a general does his soldiers. Clarke reads the force as summoned by the Almighty, its noise announcing the approach while far off. Ellicott quotes a traveller for the effect: in every stage of their existence these creatures give a most impressive view of the power of God to punish a wicked world. Calvin hears the verse answering an objection: the hearers might say great terrors are denounced as though there were no other people or forces in the world, and that if the Assyrians are formidable today they have neighbours able to raise a force to oppose them. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn that follows: there is still time to avert the completion of the judgment by sincere repentance, and Gill keeps to the plain sense of the quaking, the inhabitants shaken by the desolating judgments.
12:
The turn to repentance is read as the purpose the whole threat has been serving. Henry states it as two answers at once: thus the people would answer the end for which the judgment was sent, to convince them of sin and reduce them to their right minds and their allegiance, God bringing us into straits that he may bring us to repentance and so to himself; and thus they might stay its progress. Calvin says the same from the other end: the prophet had not intended to terrify without reason but to encourage repentance, which he could not do without offering hope of pardon, since men cannot be restored unless they entertain a hope of mercy, and one who despairs wholly disregards himself and observes no restraint. Gill fixes the timing, that this comes before the terrible day arrives and before the threatened calamities take place, and adds that serious repentance is never too late.

Ellicott makes two observations no one else makes. The word rendered saith is no common word but implies an authoritative and weighty utterance, and he quotes a commentator for the rule that it is used in almost every instance of the immediate utterance of God himself. He also notices the shape of the discourse, that the question who can abide it is left unanswered, the only possible reply being inferred from the appeal that follows. Clarke counts the means of turning that are recommended, three in number, fasting and weeping and mourning, the last being continued sorrow.

The rending of the heart rather than the garments is where the tile does its careful work, because none of them will let the comparison become a prohibition. Gill explains the custom first, that rending the garments was usual in distress as a token of grief, and insists it was neither criminal nor unlawful, the apostles having used it; it is not absolutely forbidden here but comparatively, that they should rend their hearts rather than their garments, or not their garments only but their hearts also, the outward token being one that might be done hypocritically. Clarke puts the same warning in the sharper form: merely external worship and hypocritical pretension will only increase the evil and cause God to meet them with heavier judgments. Calvin makes it a rule about ceremony: observances by which men imagine they discharge their duty are mere mockeries when a sincere heart does not precede them; God has become insensible to these customs, since toward men they are ceremonious enough and more, rending their garments and drawing pity while the heart remains untouched.

The divine attributes at the end of the verse are unpacked one by one. Clarke takes them in order: gracious means good and benevolent in his own nature; merciful means pitying and forgiving as the effect of that goodness; slow to anger follows from both, since he is not easily provoked to punish; and of great kindness means exuberant goodness to all who return to him. Wesley reduces the last clause to a line, that he turns from executing the fierceness of his wrath. Ellicott handles the repenting most carefully and states a principle: it means that of his own will he would not the death of a sinner, the judgments of God being conditional like his mercies; as it was said elsewhere that the Lord repented, that is, grieved, that he had made a certain man king, so now he repents of the evil that will fall if they are impenitent, and if they repent he may not do it. Keil and Delitzsch note where the passage is going, that to make the admonition still more emphatic the prophet concludes by repeating the appeal for the appointment of a solemn meeting.
14:
Who is the subject of the returning and repenting is disputed at the outset. Gill reports that some understand it of man, either that whoever knows the ways of repentance will return and God will then repent of the evil, which he attributes to two Jewish commentators, or that he who knows iniquity lies on him will return, the reading of a third and of the Targum. Wesley takes it of God and explains the language: God does not move from place to place, but when he withholds his blessings he is said to withdraw, and when he gives them out to return; the blessing left behind means the locusts depart before they have eaten all in the land. Clarke reads it the same way, that God may yet interpose and turn the calamity aside so far that there will be food for men and cattle and offerings enough for the temple. Ellicott makes the point precisely: the returning favour will enable the daily sacrifices to be restored, which had failed through the visitation.

Calvin faces a difficulty in the form of the words. At first sight the prophet seems to leave men perplexed, though in the previous verse he had offered hope to those who sincerely repented, so that he appears to vary his subject rather than pursue it. He states the principle at stake: all exhortations to repentance would be frigid, indeed useless, unless God also testified that he is ready to be reconciled.

The second summons to the trumpet is read as evidence of how deep the guilt ran. Calvin says the prophet reminds them of the need of deep repentance, since not individuals only but the whole people had become guilty, so it is no wonder a public profession is required; summoning assemblies by trumpet, he notes, was in common use under the law. Gill says the same briefly: this was one use of the silver trumpets made for the priests, to call the people to religious duties, that they might humble themselves and implore mercy. Henry states the transaction plainly: the priests and rulers are to appoint a solemn fast, the sinner's supplication is spare us, and God waits to be gracious; they prayed that he would spare them and he answered, since his promises are real answers to the prayers of faith and with him saying and doing are not two things. Some, he adds, understand the promises figuratively, as pointing to gospel grace.

The breadth of the summons is where the expositors are most vivid. Clarke states the rule: let all share in the humiliation, for all must feel the judgment should it come, and let no state or condition be exempted, but let all leave their houses and go to the temple. Wesley gives each class its reason. The children, though they understand little, have cries that ascend, and God with pity looks on their tears; the sucklings may move the congregation to more earnest supplication, as in the foreign city that repented at a prophet's preaching; and the newly married man is to leave the mirth of the nuptials and afflict himself with the rest. Gill takes the gathering to mean the common people, all the inhabitants summoned to seek God's face and have his judgments averted. Calvin works the philology of the word for assembly, which is not properly an assembly but the deed itself, a restraint; since it means restraint from labour as well as food it comes to designate a feast-day when men are held from work, and thence is transferred to festivals. Sanctify, he notes, seems taken here in a sense different from its earlier one. Keil and Delitzsch carry the summons forward to the priests weeping between the porch and the altar and to the prayer that follows.
17:
The place where the priests weep is fixed by three of them with some care. Gill rules out the altar of incense, which stood inside, and names the altar of burnt offering; having now nothing of that service to do, the priests are called to weep between it and the porch, where they might be seen and heard by the people in the outer court. Clarke gives the topography exactly: the altar stood before the porch with an open space of fifteen or twenty cubits between, where the priests prostrated themselves; into that space the sacrifice of atonement was brought, and there the high priest laid his hands on the victim's head while confessing sins. Wesley identifies the porch as the stately one built by the first temple's king and has the priests stand there fasting, in sight of the people in the next court.

Calvin uses the same clause for a doctrine about mediation. It was the priests' office to pray in the name of the whole people; prayer was not peculiar to them, but they prayed on behalf of all, God intending by these legal types to remind the Jews that they could not offer prayers except through a mediator, being unworthy to offer them themselves.

The reproach they pray against is read as political rather than agricultural. Ellicott observes that all mention of the locusts is dropped, the lesser calamity swallowed up in the greater; the divine reply, he adds, removes the fear that the destruction of the fruits would leave the people at the invaders' mercy. Wesley makes the comparison explicit: famine by locusts is a reproach to this heritage, but slavery to the nations the locusts signify would be greater, and on that ground the deliverance is asked.

The turn to the divine answer is marked by everyone as the hinge of the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch set out the promise as it runs, corn and new wine and oil until they are satisfied and the reproach among the nations ended. Gill glosses the jealousy as zeal for the land, for its honour and the good of its inhabitants and for the glory of God's name, with indignation moved against those who brought the desolation. Henry states the exchange as a rule of prayer: God waits to be gracious, and as soon as they humble themselves and seek his face he meets them with favours; they prayed that he would spare them, and he answered with comfortable words, his promises being real answers to the prayers of faith. Calvin makes the ground of the mercy the covenant rather than the people: God would deal mercifully with them because they were his heritage, and that title proceeds from nothing but his gratuitous covenant, the Jews being not more excellent than others.

On the tense of the answering verb Calvin enters a pointed objection. There is no reason to render it past: it stands in the same case as the verb for being jealous in the previous verse and ought like it to be future. The comment founded on the past rendering, though true in itself, is too refined and does not suit here, since the prophet is not reciting what had been done but declaring that God would be reconciled. Gill allows the past reading and a way to keep it, that God answered while they were still praying; in any case they might assure themselves he heard and would answer by words and deeds, and he reports a Jewish commentator taking the answer to come by the prophets. Clarke removes the doubt from another direction: it is no peradventure but will surely be done, and if they seek God as commanded they will find him as promised; the corn and wine mean either that the ravaging will be prevented or that the land will be blessed with such vegetable strength as to yield plentiful crops.
20:
Calling the invader the northern one is a difficulty everyone notices. Gill reports that two Jewish commentators take it of the locusts coming from the northern corner, that a third gives the same first, and that the rabbis interpret it instead of the evil imagination hidden in the heart, with the two seas mentioned afterwards standing for the two temples; he records that one of them applies the verse to the days of the Messiah. Clarke quotes a scholar for the two possibilities, that the locusts might enter by the north since two named countries abound with them, or that they are so called because they spread terror like the Assyrian armies which entered by the north; he adds that a region northward of Judea was infested with them, and that a north wind must have brought them in. Ellicott says outright that this is an exception to the usual direction of locust flight, quoting a historian for it, but holds it may be literally applied to the Assyrian hordes, whom the Jews generally spoke of as dwelling in the north, and cites the symbolic caldron in another prophet pouring its contents southward from the face of the north. Wesley keeps the locusts and divides the army topographically, the van driven into the sea east of the city and the rear into the western sea; the stench he takes either of the insects lying putrefied on the face of the earth or of the corpses of the invaders left unburied.

Calvin reads the verse as answering a fear the promise alone could not quiet. It may be that the Assyrians were by now in readiness and prepared for war, so it was difficult to free the Jews from every fear; the prophet had said generally that they would be no more subject to the mockeries of the Gentiles, yet fear could not but be felt, the people saying that they see the Assyrians already armed and can expect nothing but to be devoured. He also turns the closing clause about doing great things into a contrast: God seems for a time to lie still, withholding his power while he waits to see the tendency of the insane conspiracies and the Satanic madness of those who rise against him and his church; but having restrained himself for a time he at length comes forth, and takes his own turn to exalt himself where the invader had presumptuously attempted it.

The summons to the land and the beasts is read as a deliberate widening. Ellicott states it as a formal reversal: the sentence has gone forth, and all nature, animate and inanimate, rational and irrational, which had been included in the curse, is summoned to rejoice in the blessing. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same movement, the prophet summoning the earth and then the creatures in turn. Gill addresses the land as the land of Israel with its inhabitants, bidding them fear neither the locusts that had terrified them nor the Assyrians nor any other; on the beasts he adds a spiritual reading, that the Gentiles may be designed by them, in distinction from the children of Zion. Clarke says the words are repeated from the previous verse, God doing great things in driving the enemy away and supernaturally restoring the land to fertility. Calvin explains why beasts are addressed at all: the instruction did not suit them, but it was a more efficacious way of speaking to invite the very beasts to share the people's joy, since unless the Jews had been made to feel how far God's wrath extended, no consolation would have weighed with them. Wesley glosses the strength of the trees as bearing all they are able to stand under.
23:
The children of Zion are distinguished from the rest, and the distinction is Calvin's own. He exhorts them to rejoice in a way different from that of the land and the beasts: brute animals, while rejoicing, cannot raise their thoughts higher than their food, so that their joy terminates in its object, whereas the prophet sets God himself before the Jews as the ground of theirs. Ellicott notices the place rather than the manner, that they are called to manifest their rejoicing where the trumpet had been sounded for the fast. Gill takes them for the believing part of the people, born of Zion and brought up in her, looking for the Messiah, to whom the news of his coming would be glad tidings; he reads the joy as directed to that hope rather than to the harvest alone.

The rain given moderately is the tile's last philological knot. Clarke renders the phrase as the former rain in righteousness, that is, in due time and in just proportion, notes that this rain fell after autumn and the other in spring, and reports two renderings of the closing phrase, as aforetime on one scholar's authority and as a named month on the Syriac. Wesley distinguishes the two rains by their office, the autumn rain needed to mellow the earth and fit it to receive the corn, the latter to bring forward and ripen the fruits, so called because the husbandmen reckoned from seed time to spring and harvest, and he identifies the first month with our March. Ellicott brings in an apostle's use of rain as a witness to a pagan city of the existence and beneficence of God, who gave rain from heaven and filled hearts with food and gladness, and canvasses whether the received sense of moderately can be got out of the Hebrew at all.

Two further points are made about the season. Wesley fixes the reckoning of the husbandmen and vine-dressers, which ran from seed time to spring and harvest, so that the second rain was counted the latter. Gill and Clarke agree in taking the promise as covering both seasons together, the ground mellowed for the seed and the fruit brought to ripeness, so that the whole agricultural year is restored at once rather than a single failure repaired.
24:
The full floors and overflowing vats are read literally by two and spiritually by one. Calvin keeps to the effect of the rain: when the earth is satiated with moisture it brings forth rich fruit, so God will cause the rains not to be useless, the floors full of wheat and the vats overflowing with wine and oil. Gill allegorizes, taking the floors for the churches of Christ in Judea and among the Gentiles, set up by the preaching of the gospel under the descent of the former and latter rain, and filled with souls compared to wheat and with all spiritual provisions.

The restoration of the years is where the tile finds its most concrete natural history. Clarke recalls that the locusts destroyed not only the year's produce but so completely ate the buds and barked the trees that these did not recover for some years; the promise is that God would either prevent or remedy that evil. Ellicott says the same in a clause: the years meant are those the land would in the ordinary course of nature have needed to recover from the great army. Gill offers the alternative rendering, that God will recompense the years, giving fruitful ones as full compensation for those the locusts consumed. Calvin makes it an argument from opposites, that God can as easily restore fruitfulness as he had rendered the land barren; and he notices that four sorts are named in Hebrew as in the first chapter, one omitted here. The army is expressly called God's own so the Jews might understand that all this was in his hand.

The eating in plenty is glossed grammatically by one and doctrinally by another. Gill renders the idiom as in eating eat, and observes that the Hebraism denotes not only certainty but increase and abundance; he then turns it to the spiritual provisions held out under the gospel, much in God's goodness and faithfulness, much in his covenant, and much in Christ, who is compared to many things eatable. Clarke keeps to the occasion, praise being due for so destroying a formidable enemy and so miraculously restoring the land after a great devastation. Wesley measures the wonder arithmetically, one year giving as much as the locusts had wasted in the years before, and glosses the promise against shame as meaning they shall neither be disappointed nor forced to seek relief among the heathen.

Calvin makes the praise the proof of repentance rather than a consequence of plenty. As the Jews starved while God was offended, so when reconciled they should have abundance; but the gratitude is mentioned too, since it was evidence of true repentance when they praised the God they understood to be the giver of it, he having proved the land under his power by consuming its produce. He adds three reasons why the miracle would constrain praise: the kindness was not shown in an ordinary way, it had been foretold, and the reason given was that he was mindful of his covenant.

The presence in the midst of Israel is taken by the rest as the point the whole promise has been moving toward. Keil and Delitzsch say the people will learn thereby that God is present among them and the only true God, who does not suffer them to be put to shame, and note the rhetorical function of the repeated clause, which guarantees the grace for all ages and rounds off the section. Ellicott observes that this assurance is similar to the one with which the whole book ends, and that it prepares the way for the spiritual blessings about to be announced. Gill describes how the presence would be known: by impressions of love, the teachings of the Spirit, the usefulness of the word and ordinances, and the heavenly frame of soul, and identifies it with a blessing promised to gospel ministers.
28:
The word afterward is the hinge, and every voice reaches for the same authority. Gill dates it after the teacher of righteousness has been sent and a plentiful rain of the gospel let down in the ministry of the Baptist, of Christ and of the apostles; he reports three Jewish commentators, one saying the prophecy refers to time to come, another that the phrase is the same as in the last days, which always signifies the days of the Messiah, and notes that this is how an apostle quotes it. Clarke gives the same identification and the same rabbinic support, and adds the historical argument: there is no evidence that such an effusion took place, or such effects were produced, from the days of this prophet until the day of Pentecost. Ellicott states the principle governing the whole passage, that holy scripture is itself the interpreter of this most weighty promise and the apostle's quotation is its commentary; he tracks the changes the apostle makes, afterward becoming in his mouth in the last days, that is, in the Christian dispensation, and my Spirit rendered of my Spirit after the Greek version, indicating the gifts and influences rather than the person. Wesley dates it from the return out of Babylon and the various troubles and salvations by which they might know the Lord.

Calvin explains the order of the chapter rather than the date, and anticipates an objection to it. One may think the order irregular, since Christ reminds us that the kingdom of God is to be sought first and other things added in their place, food and everything belonging to this frail life being as it were additions to the spiritual. But the prophet designedly mentioned the evidence of God's favour in outward benefits first, because we see how slow men's perceptions are and how slothful they are in seeking spiritual life; since they rise to things above with such difficulty, he makes use of the best helps.

Henry states the same caution as a warning to the reader. The promises of corn and wine and oil in the foregoing verses would be very acceptable to a wasted country, but we are here taught that we must not rest in those things, God having reserved some better things for us; these verses have reference to those better things, both the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of glory and the happiness of true believers in each. He adds that we are at no loss about the meaning of the promise or about where it had its accomplishment, since an apostle has given an infallible explication of it.

On the reach of the phrase all flesh the expositors converge and each supplies a different reason. Ellicott takes it to mean without distinction of race or person, and cites the astonishment of those of the circumcision that the gift fell on the Gentiles also. Clarke argues it from the event, that the Spirit was poured out then on people of different countries speaking the languages of almost all the people of the earth. Wesley states the contrast historically: before, these gifts were confined to one particular nation, and now they are enlarged to all nations and all that believe. He also distinguishes two measures in the pouring, extraordinary gifts on the first preachers of the gospel and various graces to all believers, and reads the promise of prophesying as partly fulfilled to the letter in the first days but meaning further that sons and daughters shall have as full a knowledge of the mysteries of God's law as prophets had before. Keil and Delitzsch set the passage out under its own heading, the outpouring of the Spirit and the announcement of judgment, and note that the Hebrew begins a new chapter here; they refer the reader to a longer treatment in a work they name.
29:
The extension to servants and handmaids is read by everyone as the removal of a restriction, and one of them turns it into a grammatical problem. Gill has both sexes partaking of the gifts and grace of the Spirit in great abundance, many effectually called through the ministry of the word and some becoming ministers of it themselves, and he sets this expressly against a rabbinic maxim that the divine presence rests only on a man who is wise and mighty and rich. Clarke states the rule the verse establishes: the gifts of teaching and instructing men shall not be restricted to any one class or order, for God will call and qualify the men of his own choice out of all ranks and degrees and offices in society, and endow them with all the gifts and graces needed to convert sinners and build up the church. Ellicott records what an apostle draws from the same clause, that they shall prophesy, and quotes the promise made to those afar off, as many as the Lord shall call. Wesley reduces the gift to two words, the Spirit of adoption and of sanctification.

Calvin alone finds a difficulty, and it is a real one. The particle here amplifies in Hebrew, so it seems singular that the prophet should now limit to a few a gift he has just made common to all: he had said the Spirit would be poured on all flesh, and now says on servants and handmaids, with the word also attached. Had he simply said that the Spirit would be poured on servants and handmaids there would have been no inconsistency, since it would have explained the former statement; the amplifying particle is what creates the appearance of narrowing.

The wonders in heaven and earth are dated by three of them to the same event. Gill refers them to the prodigies before the destruction of Jerusalem, and reports them in detail: comets and blazing stars in the air, one in the form of a sword hanging over the city, and appearances of armies engaged in battle; and on the earth a flame seen in the temple and a voice heard in it saying, let us go hence. Clarke makes the same identification and widens the outcome, that these dreadful portents attended the final overthrow of the Jewish polity and the establishment of the Christian religion in the Roman empire, and he notes how the Lord himself applies the prophecy in the gospel. Wesley says that those who read what the historians report of those times will see this fulfilled in the very letter, and offers physical constructions for two of the signs: the blood possibly an eruption such as certain fountains have been reported to show, prefiguring the great effusion of blood by the sword and the wars following, and the fire either breaking out of the earth or lightning in the air.

Calvin, characteristically, raises the objection the sequence invites. The prophet seems here to contradict himself, since he had hitherto promised that God would deal kindly and bountifully, and everything said tended to elevate the spirits of the people and fill them with joy; yet now he seems again to threaten wrath and to strike miserable men with fear, men who had not yet had breathing time, since at the moment he spoke the Jews were in the greatest sorrow. The question of what he intends by it is the one Calvin sets himself to answer. Keil and Delitzsch supply the distinction that resolves it: it is only by the world and its children that the day of the Lord is felt as terrible, and they refer back to the earlier verses of the chapter where the same day was described.
31:
The darkened sun and bloodied moon divide the literal from the figurative, and Gill gives both. He rejects the reading of one Jewish commentator that eclipses are meant, and offers instead the clouds of smoke rising from burning towns and cities, so great as to obscure the sun and to make the moon look like blood through them. But he then supplies a figurative sense as well: the change made in the ecclesiastical and civil state of the Jewish nation, signified by the heavens and the earth, with the king or kingdom brought into a low and distressed condition under the figure of the sun, and the change of the priesthood likewise represented.

Clarke takes the figurative sense alone and states it flatly, that the Jewish polity, civil and ecclesiastical, shall be entirely destroyed. He dates the terrible day precisely, at the taking and sacking of the city and the burning of the temple by the Romans, and offers a judgment on its magnitude: this was perhaps the greatest and most terrible day of God's vengeance ever shown to the world, or that ever will be shown, until the great day of the general judgment. Wesley marks the structure of the two verses, that having mentioned the prodigies wrought on earth the prophet now specifies what shall be done in heaven, and takes the terrible day as that of the city's destruction, itself typifying the day of judgment.

Calvin argues that the whole catalogue is metaphorical and explains why it stands where it does. What is said of blood and darkness is no doubt to be taken metaphorically for a disordered state of things, since calamities are often compared to obscurity and darkness; the sense is that the succession of evils would be so great that the whole order of nature would seem subverted. He also shows how the two halves of the passage harmonize, which is the point of the arrangement: God would testify his paternal love by the manifestation of Christ, and at the same time exhibit tokens of a wrath that would fill the whole world with anxiety and fear, and both belong together in one prophecy rather than contradicting each other.
32:
The promise of deliverance to all who call is taken by every voice as the chapter's conclusion, and the expositors divide over how far it reaches. Gill gives the historical fulfilment first, that those in the city who believed had an intimation beforehand and removed to a place he names, escaping the common calamity; but he adds that the words may equally be understood of a spiritual deliverance by Christ, from sin and Satan and the world, from the second death and the wrath to come. Wesley makes the same double reading, deliverance either from those outward afflictions or, which is infinitely better, from the eternal miseries that will swallow up the unbelieving world; and he adds a remark of his own with a sharp edge, that it will aggravate the ruin of those who perish that they might have been saved on such easy terms, then turns and asks whether it is indeed easy for one not elect to repent and believe, or whether he might not as easily pull the sun out of the firmament.

Clarke works the clause philologically and then enlarges it. He gives the Hebrew and renders it all who shall invoke in the name of the Lord, and argues from an apostle's use of the verse that Christ is the Lord here meant. He reports a scholar's narrower application, that it refers to the safety of the Christians during the Jewish and Roman war, and allows that it may, but insists it has a much more extensive meaning, as the apostolic use plainly shows: every man who invokes God for mercy and salvation in the name of Jesus, that very name given under heaven among men, is included. Ellicott corrects the noun to those that escape and makes the same appeal to the apostle, who transfers the reference to the Messianic advent in order to prove the universality of the deliverance effected by one who abolished the difference between Jew and Greek; in his church, the heavenly Jerusalem freed from the persecutions and defilements of the world, there is salvation for all who call, their names inscribed on the roll as citizens of Zion.

Wesley reads the two place-names in the same key, mount Zion for the true church typified by it and Jerusalem for the mystical city of the Messiah, with the deliverance itself both temporal and eternal. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse plainly and leave the remnant clause standing as the text has it, deliverance in Zion and in Jerusalem and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.

Calvin explains the placement rather than the terms, and the explanation gathers the chapter up. The prophet had denounced future calamities in order to stimulate men, distressed by many evils, to seek God, since we know how tardy we are by nature unless the Lord goads us continually; the burden of what went before was that so many and so grievous calamities would press on the Jews that all would be miserable who did not flee to God, and that this consolation alone would remain to them in their extreme evils. Having thus stimulated them to seek him, the prophet now seasonably adds the firm assurance of being saved.
